lesson.title: The Standard Move: Step Response of First-Order Circuits
lesson.summary: Step response is the complete response of a first-order RL or RC circuit to a source that jumps suddenly from one constant value to another, and it is the single most common transient calculation in circuit analysis because switches, digital logic edges, and relay contacts all behave like step inputs.
lesson.body:
A step input is a source that holds one constant value, then at some instant t = 0 jumps abruptly to a different constant value and stays there. A battery connected through a switch is the textbook example: the source is 0 V for all time before the switch closes, then a fixed voltage for all time after. Step inputs are everywhere in real circuits, from a power supply turning on to a digital logic line flipping from low to high, which is exactly why the step response of first-order circuits gets its own name and its own standard formula rather than being treated as just one example among many of the complete response.

Because a step input is constant before and constant after the transition, its forced response is a single fixed number, found with the same open-capacitor or shorted-inductor technique used throughout this chapter, and its initial condition is whatever value the storage element held right before the switch acted. That means step response is simply the complete response template applied to this one very common, very well-behaved kind of source: x(t) = x_forced + [x(0) - x_forced] e^(-t/tau) for t >= 0, using the forced value computed after the step and the initial value that existed before it.

Work through a series RC circuit: a 9 V battery connects through a switch to a 3 kilo-ohm resistor in series with a 2 microfarad capacitor, and the capacitor starts fully discharged, so v(0) = 0 V. After the switch closes, the forced (steady-state) voltage across the capacitor equals the full source voltage, since at steady state no current flows and there is no drop across the resistor: v_forced = 9 V. The time constant is tau = RC = 3,000 ohms x 2 x 10^-6 F = 0.006 s, or 6 milliseconds. The step response is therefore v(t) = 9 - 9e^(-t/0.006) volts, matching the standard "charging" shape.

Checking specific instants confirms the exponential climb: at t = 6 ms (one time constant), v = 9(1 - e^-1) = 9 x 0.6321 = 5.689 V. At t = 12 ms (two time constants), v = 9(1 - e^-2) = 9 x 0.8647 = 7.783 V. At t = 18 ms (three time constants), v = 9(1 - e^-3) = 9 x 0.9502 = 8.552 V, well over 95 percent of the way to the 9 V destination. This 1-e^(-t/tau) shape for a rising response, and the mirror-image e^(-t/tau) shape for a falling one, are worth memorizing because they show up constantly in RC and RL analysis.

Notice how directly this connects back to first-order circuits and the complete response template covered earlier: the step response is nothing more than that same x_forced + [x(0) - x_forced]e^(-t/tau) formula, specialized to the case where x(0) and x_forced are both plain constants because the source itself is a plain constant before and after the switching instant. Nothing new is being invented here, the step response is simply the name given to the most frequently used special case.

Step response depends on the source staying at its new value forever after t = 0. Real signals rarely do that, a switch might close and then open again a few milliseconds later, which is precisely the situation the next concept, pulse response, is built to handle by treating a pulse as two steps back to back.
